Generally a very enjoyable game. The graphics are nice, the characters are entertaining, and the combat is smooth. The post-game content isn't as diverse as you would expect, but the main side-quests meant to be done are very entertaining and sufficiently difficult. Throughout the game, the skits adds perspective to the group's dynamic and world-building. There's a massive amount of these small comic-styled scenarios, and I found it very fun to find and listen to. The main locations, despite looking nice, do not feel super memorable in my opinion, only the second and third regions stood out to me. 

Though, I have some qualms with their combat system and levelling system. Some enemies feel like damage sponges despite being at the same level on Normal difficulty. It didn't exactly make the game difficult, just prolonged fights. That isn't to say the game is grindy, if you do side-quests regularly, you'll be close to pace-ish. The game tends to raise enemy levels by a couple per new area, and in some story places. It's not hard to handle a gap in levels, however. 

The first 80% of the story is a worthwhile experience. After that, it gets somewhat confusing because the pacing triples in speed, and then it's finished. Very odd, but I wouldn't say it will entirely ruin the game for you.

It took me around 15 hours to 100% it after completing the story (with post-game side-quests, collectables, and max level grinding).  

Should you buy it at full price? I wouldn't suggest it, but it is entirely worth it if it's 25% off.

I would very much like to give this game a thumbs-up. The story, setting, characters--especially the almost poetic pairing of the pain-immune Alphen and the thorn-cursed Shionne, and gameplay hold up well until you defeat the fifth lord and liberate Dahna. Then it all falls apart.

Constant cutscenes and skits, most of which say too much and accomplish too little. They clumsily rehash events and information that has only just been revealed, and do nothing to move the story forward or develop the characters. There's one or two interesting reveals in there, as well as a few cutscenes that pay off on the hours you've spent getting there, but it's a whole lot of nothing happening.

Honestly, the game should have ended after you liberate Dahna. But their premise of Renans arriving on Dahna from spaceships demanded a reckoning, and the developers and writers hadn't an ounce of creative energy left so they put the answers to any possible outstanding questions into a computer terminal and made you fight mid-tier bosses as field enemies in the final dungeon for 2+ hours before bringing back a middle-game boss for the end. Why? I dunno, just because.

The story is obviously too long for the vehicle it's delivered in, though not because it needed to be. The back half of the game is two or three hours of content stretched out to 10+ for....no reason at all. And the result? Not enough enemies to keep the gameplay refreshing. Not enough world to explore as you uncover the truths you've been seeking. Not enough character development for me to give a damn about anything that doesn't feature Alphen and Shionne.

And let's give special mention to the final dungeon. I'm the first nor last to mention how long and tedious it is. After a while I started seeing enemies in front of doorways and thinking "Oh, okay, the developers want me to spend 10-15 minutes here," because that's truly the only reason the enemies are there. Yes, you can flee from them if you want, but you'll be punished for it by being underlevel when you start the final boss. That's not to say you can't win, if you play well enough or lower the difficulty. The point is, the game had long since stopped being designed around delivering a story sandwiched with Action/RPG gameplay. It had reduced itself to time-gating the player so it didn't seem "too short" and just ended up branding itself as "not fun" in the end. And in the final dungeon the devs made zero effort to even hide this fact. Here you go, eight more instances of boss-as-field-enemy. Have fun.

At least the ending is somewhat satisfying, if you're a fan of the good ol' deus ex machina, despite the slog to get there. I've no shame in admitting I turned on OHK in cheat engine to get there. Why? Because fighting a giant lizard for the first and second time was kind of cool. The fifteenth? Not so much.

I honestly really liked the first two-thirds of the game; The plot was generic but enjoyable, the characters were cliche but likable, the combat was repetitive but satisfying, and the graphics and music were not special but still great. The game wasn't perfect, but it was fun and I was excited for more.

Everything is a downward spiral once you meet the 4th lord. The dialogue/writing devolves into infuriating anime tropes that genuinely pissed me off more and more as the game went on. It feels like the devs switched writers at this point because the drop in quality was way too blatant. The combat also became way worse for the rest of the game by spamming damage-sponge enemies at you (this isn't difficult or challenging, it's just mind-numbingly tedious) and areas also become way more tedious with unnecessary backtracking. For the final sections of the game, everything gameplay-wise feels like wasting time and everything story-wise feels frustrating.

At the time of writing i have 22 hours and 45 minutes of playtime as listed on the save file and playing on normal difficulty but I have not completed the game and I can not in good faith recommend this game to anyone. Even fans of the Tales of series. 

[b]Enemy Scaling [/b]
 Starting with the gameplay issues first it is pretty obvious that the balance is designed with the level up pack DLC in mind. The way normal enemies are scaled vs bosses is absurd with some bosses needing at least a some grinding to be able to level up to beat and then after the boss is defeated the common enemy level drops off and the game becomes a cake walk until the next boss where the process repeats itself.

[b]Cure Points [/b]
I want to love the cure points system but the implementation is just feels wrong. Having no mana and just having a pool of healing for the entire team is a great concept but despite being called Cure Points, CP, these points are used for all of your world interactions points as well such as knocking out a wall of fire or ice. This makes the already rare/expensive orange gel even more valuable unless you want to ignore these special points and come back later on a return visit but coming back to late will cause most of the items to be worthless to you. CP would have been better off just being exclusively for healing and not tying it to world interactions.

[b] Currency [/b]
  Next on the list is gald, the currency of the game. Compared to any other game in the series, as long as you didnt wildly burn though your supplies, you were able to keep up with the flow of the game without depleting everything you have. In this game however, your NPC allies will burn though everything you have except life bottles in no time flat if you keep the default strategy untill you have 4 remaining which creates a huge issue of burning though all of your gald to make sure you have the supplies to take on the boss. For myself i use the "No item" strategy for anything other than bosses and when I start a boss encounter I change to the "Go all out" strategy. This helps the gald situation a little bit but income is very low and orange gels, which restore 30% of your ability to heal without using items, cost a whopping 3000gald each. Kinda convenient that there are not 1 but 4 gald packs available to purchase yeah?

   Writing.... Oh boy where do I begin with the writing... Its not great. At very few points do I feel like characters are growing and the times I did they were beginning to grow it was completely unwritten not long after. A character even points this out to them which says to me even the writers of the game agree the characters are not growing. The game is also very consistent in the tropes the writers want to use, falling back over and over and over again on the same tropes but with a slightly different coat of paint.

  The voice acting is.. fine? A few of the characters don't have a range of emotion in most situations that would call for them.

[b]Combat[/b]
   Combats fun if you play as any of the martial characters. Magic was absolutely gutted in this game to the point that Rinwell, the mage, performs better as a martial than a mage. As for everything else, there is room for improvement but it's not something that I feel needs to be called out.

[b]Graphics [/b]
The graphics look fine 
[b]DLC [/b]
Now... Lets talk DLC shall we because my god is it bad. If all this game did was offer costumes and accessories I would be completely fine with that but it doesnt it offers the entire game to you. Now i know offering levels and items isn't new to the Tales of series but in this iteration these packs are advertised to you in a number of places and even while making camp. [b]**IT IS EVEN POSSIBLE THAT THE GAME WILL SPOIL A MAJOR PLOT EVENT FOR YOU ON YOUR FIRST REST WITH THE ADS.**[/b] It's so unholy unnecessary and feels really bad to see. 
Next is the $85 and $110 version of the game. WHAT THE ACTUAL FUCKING IS THIS SHIT. HOW do you sell 3 different tiers of a game and NOT list whats in them? HOW do you lock character progression behind this kind of paywall at this point in gaming. This shit is awful and in no way should be tolerated by anyone in gaming.

-No native controller support but thats not the biggest issue if steam's controller support works for you.
-The inability to return to the title screen to exit the game is reallllly strange. Needing to alt+f4 to close the game baffles me. (or im really dumb and cant find it.)

[b]Conclusion [/b]
I wanted so much more from this game. The concepts and gameplay seems great but the execution was just so poor from a writing and management perspective. Playing through it's super obvious where the higher ups told designers where to change things to incentivize players to buy DLC. I'm going to continue to try and play though the game and see it to the end but at this point I am not enjoying the process.

As for the good parts of the game, I found the gameplay and art direction to be the best parts. The game looks great from the varied landscapes, vistas, and most of the character designs. Unlocking new abilities and learning the character abilities to counter mobs and bosses adds some depth to the fast-paced gameplay and made the gameplay a highlight to me, even if there may be too many mob fights at times in dungeons. The music seems better to me than the other Tales games I’ve played and while it’s not too big of a standout of a soundtrack compared to other games, it’s still a good one. I felt that the production quality of the game was better than other Tales games too so I appreciate the higher quality cutscenes, facial + hair animations, and even animated parts of the game. While not especially interesting, I always like how Tales games handle the equipment system. It’s basic (i.e. numbers go up and new weapon models), but it works well enough with getting stronger gear by finding it in the environment, crafting it, or buying from a vendor. I think the difficulty is done well enough too although the game is clearly not made for the hardest difficulty and even struggles on ‘Challenging’ mode as I played most of the game on 'Challenging' but I had to turn it down on certain parts because the companion AI simply couldn’t dodge well enough and I’d resort to item spam to survive, which makes the combat more tedious and annoying than rewarding and skill-based.
 
As for the bad parts, there’s a lot. Given that this was one of the highest rated Tales games, I went in with expectations and was severely underwhelmed. The world feels fake within the first hour due to poor world-building and while I hoped it would get better (as alot of JRPGS are slow in the beginning) after several hours, it doesn’t. It’s a mixture of bad + basic writing, characters acting ridiculous to cause drama, and the story creating plot twists out of nowhere. The plot is filled with writing shortcuts, some plot twists being painfully obvious in some cases while in others, there's plot elements that make more questions than answers. Additionally, near the end of the game, there is far too much story + lore-dumping where it really had lose patience. I’m used to Tales games stories falling apart at the midway point or 2/3rds, but I genuinely only enjoyed one region’s story and even that one struggled near the end of that arc. Anyway, regarding the cast, the characters don’t help the game that much as while I enjoyed some parts of the cast, I’m very mixed on them as characters since most have such unlikeable character traits for the majority of the game. Especially Shionne. I generally like Tales casts as they usually have 1-2 party members that stand out as well-written, 1-2 that are somewhat good, and then the rest that are okay or throwaway characters. But, not Arise’s. This is a story-based character action-RPG so you really need to either string gameplay, a strong cast of characters, or a strong story for a 50-hr main story. Preferably all three. So the fact that Arise only does a good job in gameplay is a massive downer for me. 

As for the expansion, it’s okay at best. It’s a premium-priced expansion but it feels like it was made on a budget. You can’t carry over weapons previously crafted nor your levels from the base game (for balancing purposes, I suppose), several repeated + reskinned bosses/enemy mobs from the base game, and the same basic writing and okay quest design. It’s very bland as it’s more of the same and doesn’t fix, or improve upon, any of the many issues that I had with the base game. Possibly worst of all, it doesn’t add new abilities, weapons, or combat artes to the combat system. This would be a no-brainer to add since the combat is the game’s strongest aspect. The dlc isn’t worth the cost at full price or on discount and to be frank, I don’t know why it was even made besides spending more time with the cast. When you compare this expansion's quality and length to some other AAA-games that have pricey expansions, it’s baffling.  

Overall, it’s one of the biggest disappointments I’ve had in recent memory, especially considering the praise this game had received in 2021. I enjoyed it for a person who likes the Tales games that I’ve played but I expected much more. I’m a person who grew up with Symphonia on GameCube and Vesperia on 360 so given that it’s been 15-20 years between Arise and those titles, I expected a far bigger jump in progression. Granted, Arise does do things better than those titles for sure (to name a few things: fast travel, side quests are no longer hidden, titles have more of a purpose, and all characters are more viable to play solo) but I found Arise’s faults just too big for me to prefer Arise over Vesperia/Symphonia. The gameplay and visuals are the main selling points. I do recommend it at a heavily discounted price if you want a light-hearted JRPG romp with some good visuals, good combat, and some funny moments. The expansion knocks the score down a bit down as it felt like a waste of time. 7.0/10.

[h2]An Epic Tale of Freedom and Unity[/h2]
[i]Tales of Arise[/i] is a captivating JRPG that combines classic series traditions with modern innovations. From an emotional storyline to dynamic gameplay, it offers an engaging journey that appeals to both veterans of the series and newcomers alike. It’s not necessary to have played previous [i]Tales of[/i] games to understand the story or characters.

[h3]Story[/h3]
In a world where the people of Dahna suffer under the tyranny of the neighboring planet Rena, an unnamed masked hero rises to fight for freedom. Alongside a mysterious woman cursed by her powers, the group stands against their oppressors, uncovering a larger threat that endangers both worlds.

[h3]Strengths[/h3]
[b]✔️ Compelling Storyline:[/b]
[i]Tales of Arise[/i] delivers a powerful tale of oppression, rebellion, and unity. The themes of freedom and understanding are emotionally gripping and keep players invested until the end.

[b]✔️ Impressive Visuals:[/b]
The anime-inspired art style, detailed environments, and vibrant character designs create an immersive and breathtaking experience.

[b]✔️ Dynamic Combat System:[/b]
The action-packed and fluid combat system is both challenging and rewarding, allowing for creative use of Artes and Boost Strikes.

[b]✔️ Memorable Characters:[/b]
Each character has a unique personality, intriguing backstory, and crucial role in the narrative, making the journey feel personal and meaningful.

[b]✔️ Outstanding Soundtrack:[/b]
The music perfectly enhances every moment, from epic battles to emotional story beats, and stays with you long after playing.

[h3]Weaknesses[/h3]
[b]❌ Repetitive Environments:[/b] 
Some areas feel less inspired and can become repetitive, especially during extended exploration.

[b]❌ Difficulty Spikes:[/b]
The first major boss fight can be exceptionally challenging, even on the lowest difficulty setting.

[b]❌ Grindy Endgame:[/b]
Completing optional content or preparing for tougher challenges involves repetitive tasks, which might deter casual players.

[h3]Achievements[/h3]
There are 58 achievements available here. To unlock all of them, you’ll need the [i]Tales of Arise - Beyond the Dawn[/i] expansion. The achievements span the main story, optional bosses, and various gameplay-specific challenges. These include finding all the owls, unlocking all recipes, and mastering the training grounds. While none of the achievements are missable, the endgame can require significant time and patience, particularly for the tougher challenges.

[h3](Not) Recommended for[/h3]
[b]✔️ Recommended for[/b]
• Fans of story-driven RPGs with emotional depth.
• Players who enjoy action-packed combat with strategic elements.
• Fans of beautifully animated cutscenes and exceptional voice acting.

[b]❌ Not Recommended for[/b]
• Players expecting a fully open-world sandbox experience.
• Those who dislike grind-heavy or highly challenging content.

[h3]Final Verdict[/h3]
[I]Tales of Arise[/i] is a shining example of what a modern JRPG can achieve. It blends the classic charm of the series with contemporary gameplay innovations and is a must-play for both fans and newcomers. Despite the difficulty spikes, the overall experience remains unforgettable. 😊

I'm writing this review at about 30 hours into the game.  I'd normally wait until the end to share my thoughts but I've reached a point in the game where I'm losing motivation to finish it and may not make it all the way through.

The game has fantastic gameplay with below average writing and characters.  My issues are not with the tropes or the cliches, but with the actual plot, setting, character motivations, and character development.  I believe I could accurately boil down every character into a single sentence without losing any depth in the process.  That could be totally fine if the writers actually chose to lean into the identities they gave to their characters, but 90% of the game's skits and cutscenes seem to be generic anime filler rather than meaningful character interaction.  It feels like there are different writers involved in the story bits than there are in the rest of the game, and nobody wants to play it 'risky' by developing any of the characters out of turn.

Speaking of separate writing teams, I'm certain there were at least three separate writers in charge of writing for Shionne in the first few hours of the game.  Her tone changes from scene to scene and her battle dialog doesn't line up with her victory dialog or her story dialog.  The plot dialog is similarly jumbled in tone as the game progresses.  We start with the main characters determined to "take down the lords" and end slavery.  At one point they see a bunch of people happy and reconsider the entire plot of the game for about an hour before the game forces them to reconsider their reconsideration.  Then you get a boss fight with a character the plot doesn't even need you to fight, because I guess we needed a boss fight, and after that boss fight everyone acts like it was totally fine that this character you literally came to town to murder just tried to murder all of you.  About ten hours later we even get one of those fun "Rose" cutscenes similar to the end of The Last Jedi, where someone on your team is about to kill a villain and someone else on your team decides the heroic thing to do is step inbetween them and almost die saving the bad guy.  You would imagine this means the bad guy wasn't actually all that bad, right?  No, no, it was because the good guy was too angry when she attacked the bad guy, and her friend didn't want her to kill the bad guy angry.  So he risked killing himself and traumatizing her to save the bad guy to stop her from getting her revenge on the evil bad guy.

At the end of that fight the whole team decides to chase and kill the bad guy that good guy just saved.  That's where the writing is in this game.  It's wherever it wants to be.  The characters just follow along and say whatever needs to be said to make the plot happen.  It isn't just 'generic,' or just 'anime,' or just 'JRPG' writing.  It's spectacularly, embarrassingly terrible writing.  It doesn't feel like it was 'made for kids,' it feels like it was made by some kind of anime trope algorithm.

Tales games aren't really the place to go for 'mature' or 'deep' writing but Tales of Berseria impressed me with its characters and its treatment of 'good' and 'evil.'  The gameplay isn't up to par with Arise but if you really want to play something kinda like this, with some actual characters and plot points that you might carry around with you when you're done playing, try that.

This is my 3rd Tales game after Berseria and Zestiria. Played the game start to finish. The game is technically great but I [i]almost[/i] couldn't recommend it after finishing it. 

The pros:
+ Fighting mobs is fun. Executing Boost Strikes is always flashy and feels good.
+ They nailed that adventuring feel with camping and cooking.
+ Characters are nowhere near Berseria level of good but they're still [i]mostly[/i] good. Alphen and Shionne takes the cake here.
+ I like the Cure Points mechanic being a resource you have to refill by camping. 

The cons:
- [i]The dumbest AI I have ever seen in any video game[/i]. It doesn't matter what kind of strategy you set for them, they will keep dying to some boss attacks. They're fine at the start but as the game's combat grows more complex with group fights and AoEs they'll struggle to keep up.
- For some reason someone at Bamco thought Tales should play like a Souls game and everyone can only dodge (and one character can only block, not dodge). Everything now hits like a freight train, combine that with the AI stupidity earlier and everyone's gonna keep dying, draining your resources.
- Fighting mobs is fun, but fighting bosses feels like playing a different game. The large monsters are cancer. They can't be staggered outside of Boost Attacks AND they spam big attacks halfway through their health bar and you have to awkwardly wait for your Boosts to refill and counter. The human bosses are fine though, they're fun.
- Toward the end of the game basically everything that made it fun gets dropped. [spoiler]No camping, no cooking, plot expositions everywhere and you're walking in these generic sci-fi hallways. The party became so straight-laced and boring, I found myself rooting for Vholran the peak hater. At least the ending's pretty.[/spoiler]

6/10, It's a decently polished game but it just has a lot of sore points you see every now and then. I got this on a sale in a bundle with Scarlet Nexus and [i]that[/i] one ended up surprisingly being the funner experience. Just get it on a sale, or get Berseria instead if you haven't played that one.

In a sentence: this is a good game. Just stop playing the moment you achieve the goal your party gives itself after the first chapter; that's where it should have ended.
The rest of the story makes no sense and the final dungeons feel added on at best - like EX content they made part of the main story because it wasn't long enough. To put it plainly, this game could have been much better without a twist and just focusing on the goal it provides the player at the start of the game.
